en.title: A Comprehensive Guide to the Smart Typer Pro App
en.summary: Smart Typer Pro is an all-in-one productivity app for Android devices that completely redefines mobile note-taking, text editing, voice dictation, artificial intelligence assistance, and document…
en.body:
Published 15 August 2026 by Syed Sharib Ali

Smart Typer Pro is an all-in-one productivity app for Android devices that completely redefines mobile note-taking, text editing, voice dictation, artificial intelligence assistance, and document management. Rather than operating as a basic text editor or a single simple tool, Smart Typer Pro serves as a central, easy-to-use digital workspace designed for everyone—from everyday users, students, and writers to content creators and users who rely on accessibility features.

This comprehensive guide breaks down every single feature, setting, handy customization, system integration, and daily shortcut inside Smart Typer Pro in clear, easy-to-understand detail.

Download the app on Google Play

Table of Contents

Smart Typer Pro keeps all your work neat, organized, and easy to find on your Android phone or tablet. When you open the app, it automatically creates a main folder named Smart Typer directly in your device’s main internal storage root ( /sdcard/Smart Typer ).

Located at the bottom-right corner of the main screen, the Plus (+) / Create button lets you create new items instantly:

Located at the top-right of the main screen:

By default, long-pressing (holding down) any file or folder brings up a comprehensive context menu loaded with quick actions tailored specifically to the file type:

When you turn on multi-select mode (or select multi-file options), you can handle several items together:

The built-in editor screen is the heart of Smart Typer Pro. It handles everything from quick daily scratch notes to large document files smoothly.

Smart Typer Pro makes typing hands-free easy with voice dictation built straight into the text editor.

Set up custom shorthand phrases in Settings. For example:

While you speak, Smart Typer Pro automatically detects your custom shortcuts and expands them into full sentences instantly.

Smart Typer Pro offers four writing assistant options to refine your notes according to your needs:

The AI Typing Assistant screen offers a dedicated, distraction-free space for dictating text, polishing ideas with AI, and sharing messages directly.

Available from the main menu side drawer and directly from the text editor’s More Options menu, the Quick AI Assistant gives you a friendly, helpful AI chat companion ready to answer questions or help write content.

The Text-to-Handwriting feature turns your digital text notes into realistic handwritten PDF files or image pages.

Smart Typer Pro uses high-quality realistic voice technology to convert your text documents into clear, natural-sounding MP3 audio files. Conveniently access this feature directly from the long-press file context menu ( Convert to Audio ) as well as from the Smart Utilities Hub.

Smart Typer Pro includes built-in pop-up media players so you can listen to audio recordings or watch video clips without needing separate apps.

The Media Scanner tool quickly scans your phone to organize and show all your media files in one clean dashboard.

The Instant Translator tool offers fast, multi-language document translation. Access it conveniently from the Smart Utilities Hub , the long-press file context menu ( Translate Text ), or directly inside the text editor’s More Options menu while working on a note.

The Wikipedia Search tool lets you research topics and extract information right inside the app. Access it from the Smart Utilities Hub or directly while editing notes via the text editor’s More Options menu.

Word Helper uses AI to turn any word or phrase into a comprehensive, easy-to-understand dictionary guide. Access it from the Smart Utilities Hub or directly while writing notes via the text editor’s More Options menu.

The Smart Utilities Hub acts as a central control panel holding all 12 main tools of Smart Typer Pro (including Instant Language Translator, Wikipedia Search, Quick AI Assistant, Word Helper, and Text-to-Audio).

The Settings screen gives you full control over how Smart Typer Pro works:

Smart Typer Pro fits naturally into your daily Android phone routine.

Smart Typer Pro is set up to handle standard file actions across your system:

Disclaimer: This guide was provided by the Smart Typer Pro developers. It was not written or independently reviewed by the Accessible Android team.

Published in Tutorials

en.body:
Published 14 August 2026 by Syed Sharib Ali

Smart Typer is a lightweight yet feature-rich Android productivity application designed to bring notes, file management, advanced text editing, AI tools, and everyday utilities into a single workspace. It allows users to create, edit, organize, copy, move, rename, share, and convert files while also providing an integrated file manager for browsing and managing device storage.

Its powerful text editor supports both regular writing and coding, with features such as Find & Replace, precise text splitting, multi-selection, voice typing, offline voice-input correction, Markdown/blog writing, and multiple AI-powered text refinement modes. Users can also translate text, look up words with Word Helper, search and read Wikipedia articles, and convert text into PDF, realistic handwriting, or natural-sounding audio.

Smart Typer also includes an AI Companion for answering questions with beautifully formatted responses, an AI Typing Assistant, Archive Viewer for ZIP/RAR files, image, audio, video, and Markdown viewers, and enhanced Microsoft Word document support. With extensive customization, tablet and landscape support, and compatibility with numerous text and document formats, Smart Typer aims to provide a versatile productivity environment for students, writers, developers, professionals, and everyday Android users.

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

The UI is designed with accessibility in mind and works with prominent Android screen readers, including TalkBack, CSR, and PSR. Interactive buttons and controls are properly labelled, and accessibility actions are provided where applicable, including for file and folder operations. Screen-reader navigation is supported throughout the app, with particular attention given to accessible text editing, file management, and utility workflows. No significant unlabeled-button or accessibility issues are currently known.

en.title: Unboxr
en.summary: Unboxr is the ultimate lightweight and secure tool for extracting archives on your Android device. Designed with a beautiful, modern dark theme using Jetpack Compose,…
en.body:
Published 9 August 2026 by Warren Carr

Unboxr is the ultimate lightweight and secure tool for extracting archives on your Android device. Designed with a beautiful, modern dark theme using Jetpack Compose, Unboxr makes managing compressed files fast and intuitive.

Key Features:

Free or paid:

Accessibility and User Comments:

“Unboxr” is a simplistic app intended for extracting compressed files, with support for several formats, including password-protected archives.

The UI is straightforward, with an “Open Folder” button that, when tapped, takes you to your phone’s internal storage, where you can choose the location containing the file you want to extract. The app also appears among the apps that can handle these file types, so you can select supported files from a file manager without using the dedicated button in the app.

In the top-right corner, there is a “Settings” button where you can customize the app. The customization options are quite limited, though. The Settings section also includes a donation option at the very bottom of the screen labeled “Buy me a coffee”

The app is completely free and contains no ads.

The app is very minimalistic. I noticed that it is not possible to make the app ask you where you want the contents to be saved every time you extract a file, despite the presence of an “Always ask” option in Settings, which, based on its explanation, should enable this behavior. Instead, to select the output directory, you have to specify it through the “Default destination folder” option.

When it comes to accessibility, I didn’t encounter any issues with the app.

Last Tested App version and Android version:

v1.0. Android 16

en.body:
We’re getting ever closer to NVDA 2026.2 and we hit a new milestone towards that this week. Let’s have a look at what’s in this week’s blog and then dive in:

NVDA 2026.2 is nearly here! This week we’re up to NVDA 2026.2 Beta 10 . We are now in the “String freeze” – that is, we don’t make any changes for a couple of weeks to give the translators time to update their work before the stable release. So, the next step should be a release candidate in a couple of weeks. Then, all going to plan, the final release a week or so after that. Let’s have a look at the updates from the betas since the last In-Process:

Changes introduced in NVDA 2026.2 Beta 10 : Updates to translations Fixed touchscreen, touchpad and mouse input for magnifier Added gestures for braille automatic scroll commands Removed True Center Mode and Border Mode from the magnifier due to design bugs Remove non-functional “Custom” option from the math decimal separator setting

Changes introduced in Beta 9: Updates to translations Update Braille Reading and Automatic Scroll Rate in User Guide Moving by sentence in Word (alt+downArrow/alt+upArrow) at the start/end of a document now stops there instead of wrapping around to the opposite end Changed quick access keys for magnifier settings to ensure they are unique Changes introduced in Beta 8: Updates to translations Improve magnifier behaviour when using higher DPI scaling Fix magnifier from interfering with opening dictionary dialogs Improve the handling of failing to activate the magnifier Block touch screen input when using the magnifier where possible, as it is not supported yet

We try to ensure there are plenty of ways for NVDA users to get help. Since you’re reading this blog post, I HOPE you would consider our blog one of the ways you learn more about NVDA. We have training material and telephone support in our shop, and they are both very popular options (particularly combined in the NVDA Productivity Bundle ). But what about in NVDA itself? There are a couple of ways you can get help while you are using NVDA: The User Guide. (And particularly the quick start guide for new users). The user guide contains information on all of the features of NVDA. It is an excellent resource to refer back to after completing “ Basic Training for NVDA ” and learning about all the features. Press NVDA+n to open the NVDA menu, then h for the help submenu, which starts on the User Guide The other items in the “Help” menu for information including what is new , links to the NV Access website , help and training , and the “ Commands quick reference ” (the tables of keystrokes and gestures extracted from the user guide). Context sensitive help. From within any dialog in NVDA, press f1 to open the user guide to the topic on the current control. Input Help. Press NVDA+1 (the 1 in the number row, above Q). In this mode, NVDA will report any key that you press. If you press an NVDA command (such as NVDA+tab), it will report that. Keys pressed and commands are not executed. This can be a great way of exploring a new keyboard layout. Press NVDA+1 again to turn input help off. Report keystroke: While we’re on help for individual keys, the Report Keystroke command tells you the keystroke to access the currently focussed control. Press shift+numpad 2 (laptop: NVDA+control+shift+dot ) to report the keystroke for the current control .

The WebAIM screen reader user’s survey is on again. This is the 11th edition of the survey, which is the largest survey we are aware of which collects data on screen reader usage and trends. We encourage everyone to complete it in order to give the community as accurate a picture of how you use a screen reader as possible!

The one question I’d like to highlight is “ Screen reader satisfaction ”. Please do answer all the questions honestly, including that one – but if there is anything which makes you think “I’m not 100% satisfied with NVDA” – please let us know! You can create an issue on GitHub (and we’ve previously included GitHub instructions here in In-Process , you can email us , reach us in the official NVDA mailing list , or on social media .

We are very grateful to all our donors . They are one of the main reasons we are able to continue to provide NVDA for free to anyone who can use it anywhere in the world.

This week, we’d like to give a shoutout to Acapela who make the popular Acapela TTS for NVDA . If you are interested in trying Acapela out, they offer an evaluation version which is fully functional and provides access to all voices and all functionalities for 15 days.

Acapela, along with many other options, are listed on our Extra Voices page .

And, if you would like to donate and help keep NVDA free for everyone, we would welcome your support. Please visit our donation page for PayPal or bank donation options. You can also become a GitHub Sponsor .

One of the fixes in the recent NVDA 2026.2 betas is a fix to moving by sentences in Microsoft Word. In many places in Microsoft Office, you can press alt+down arrow to move to the next sentence and alt+up arrow to move to the previous sentence. While this is a feature of Office, if you appreciate moving by sentence and would like to be able to use it everywhere, try out the “ Sentence Nav ” add-on in the add-on store.

Want more ways of getting around? How about: Word ( control+left arrow and control+right arrow ) Paragraph ( control+up arrow and control+down arrow OR shift+p and p ) And as an added bonus for paragraph navigation, here’s a related feature: Paragraph style , which lets you change how NVDA moves when moving by paragraph Single letter navigation What other ways do you prefer to navigate documents? Continue the conversation on social media .

That’s all for this week. Next time around we’ll be close to the final 2026.2 release, so for now, do try out the latest beta and be sure to report any issues. Also don’t forget to do the WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey .

es.summary: Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación, la beta 10 de NVDA 2026.2 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, … Continuar leyendo "Ya disponible la décima beta de NVDA 2026.2" La entrada Ya disponible la décima beta de NVDA 2026.2 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .
es.body:
Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación , la beta 10 de NVDA 2026.2 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, o por el sistema de informe de fallos de NV Access . Esta versión no es apta para entornos de producción. Al instalar esta beta te unirás al canal beta, y sólo recibirás avisos de actualización de compilaciones beta y candidatas a liberación (rc). El canal beta/rc siempre te mantendrá al día con la versión más reciente de NVDA. La última rc de un ciclo de liberación es idéntica a la última versión estable. Para regresar al canal de versiones estables, instala a mano la última versión estable.

Esta versión incluye una nueva función de ampliación, mejoras en los gestos táctiles y la navegación, y capacidades mejoradas de voz y braille. El ampliador proporciona opciones de zoom y filtro de color para asistir a usuarios con baja visión. Actualmente, el ampliador sólo soporta el modo a pantalla completa, dejando los modos acoplados planificados para una futura versión. Se ha expandido significativamente el soporte táctil con nuevos gestos de pellizcar y con navegación en modo exploración táctil en contenido web. Ahora se puede navegar por enlaces, encabezados, campos de formulario y otros elementos usando deslizamientos táctiles. Se han mejorado las funciones de voz con soporte de diccionarios del habla personalizados que pueden proporcionarse en complementos y nuevos tipos de entradas de diccionario que proporcionan un control más granular. Se ha añadido una nueva opción en las voces OneCore para controlar las pausas después de la puntuación. Una nueva orden permite repetir la última información verbalizada, con la capacidad de mostrarla en un mensaje explorable. El gesto predeterminado para repetir la última información verbalizada es NVDA+x, y se puede cambiar desde el diálogo Gestos de entrada. La pantalla braille ahora puede desplazarse automáticamente, y los dispositivos DotPad soportan combinaciones multibotón. Liblouis se ha actualizado con nuevas tablas braille en italiano y estonio. Al restablecer NVDA a los valores de fábrica, ahora hay disponible un botón de deshacer para restaurar la configuración anterior. Para instalar esta beta, puedes configurar el canal «rc y beta» en el complemento Selector del canal de actualización y buscar actualizaciones desde el menú Ayuda de NVDA, o actualizar desde una beta anterior. Y como siempre, también puedes descargar manualmente el instalador de NVDA 2026.2 beta 10 . Su suma de comprobación SHA256, que te permitirá garantizar la integridad del archivo descargado, es 027c1b5a1d6024288ffc672f601069856aaa75de1b8600ce40ce5beceb623306. ¡Feliz jueves!

La entrada Ya disponible la décima beta de NVDA 2026.2 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .

en.summary: Talk Forward is a powerful screen reader that makes your Android phone and tablet fully usable by voice and touch — built for blind and…
en.body:
Published 3 August 2026 by Yannick Plassiard

Talk Forward is a powerful screen reader that makes your Android phone and tablet fully usable by voice and touch — built for blind and low-vision users who want speed, control, and modern features.

Refined for responsiveness, Talk Forward focuses on what matters most: fast, reliable feedback and deep customization, so the device works the way you do.

KEY FEATURES

Talk Forward is built with and for its community, and improves continuously based on real user feedback.

ACCESSIBILITY NOTE

Talk Forward uses Android’s accessibility services to read screen content aloud and let you control your device entirely by touch and gestures. This access is used only to provide screen-reader functionality on your device.

Accessibility and User Comments:

User feedback plays a central role in the development of Talk Forward. Reports, suggestions, and real-world experiences help improve performance, compatibility, speech feedback, gestures, and overall usability across different Android devices and apps.

Last Tested App version and Android version:

26.8.1. Android 16

es.body:
Disponible el número 49 de “Arroba Sonora”, el podcast de tecnología del CTI, que puede descargarse desde el Gestor ONCE de Libros Digitales, el ClubONCE o escucharse a través de las principales plataformas de podcast o desde la Web del CTI.

En este número se comienza hablando de un producto que, aunque no ha sido diseñado específicamente para personas con ceguera o deficiencia visual grave, destaca por sus interesantes posibilidades de uso y su accesibilidad. Se trata de un escáner portátil de la marca Brother , capaz de digitalizar hojas sueltas y que incorpora funciones como escaneo mediante Wifi, almacenamiento en tarjetas de memoria y una aplicación de gestión con un notable nivel de accesibilidad.

Con motivo del próximo eclipse total de Sol del 12 de agosto se conversa con Enrique Pérez Montero, astrofísico del Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía en Granada, quien comentará algunos de los aspectos más interesantes de este fenómeno astronómico. Además, dará a conocer iniciativas y recursos relacionados con la astronomía accesible, acercando la ciencia y la observación del universo a todas las personas.

Se informa también de la existencia de Tactonom, un dispositivo diseñado para facilitar el acceso a contenidos táctiles e interactivos. Durante la entrevista se dará a conocer qué es, cuáles son sus principales funcionalidades, a quién va dirigido y qué aplicaciones prácticas puede tener tanto en el ámbito educativo como en otros entornos de aprendizaje.

El contenido íntegro de Arroba Sonora en formato texto puede descargarse desde el Gestor ONCE de Libros Digitales, o consultarse en la sección correspondiente, de “Arroba Sonora”, dentro de la Web del CTI.

en.title: In-Process 20th July 2026
en.summary: Welcome to a new week and a new edition of the blog! There’s a few things inside, starting off with very sad news of the passing of a legend of the community. Vale Rui Fontes NVDA 2026.2 Beta 7 Characters per line Introducing Access Point System Accessibility Repair Tool Vale Rui Fontes Last week, we… Read More
en.body:
Welcome to a new week and a new edition of the blog! There’s a few things inside, starting off with very sad news of the passing of a legend of the community.

Last week, we were saddened to receive news of the passing of longtime friend of the NVDA community, and of NV Access, Rui Fontes. Rui was a prominent face of “Tiflotecnia”, the organisation who sell Vocalizer for NVDA. Rui was a very prominent add-on developer. There are 16 current add-ons in the store published by him, including the very popular SysTrayList, ClipSpeak and TesseractOCR being just three, as well as contributing to numerous others. Rui was also very active in the NVDA user group, add-on group and other forums, and very interested in helping people in general, not only with his products. He was a tireless advocate for the community. He will be greatly missed. His family have asked for privacy at this time. Please also refrain from asking about his add-ons. Rest assured, they will continue to work throughout the NVDA 2026.x year cycle, even without any additional updates. No doubt, accommodations will be made for their future long before NVDA 2027.1 comes out, and we will share any additional news as we receive it.

Over the weekend, the community received a message from Rui’s wife and daughters deeply thank all those who expressed their condolences regarding the passing of their beloved one, who will remain eternally in our memories. Be sure to subscribe to the official NVDA users email group , or the add-on group for updates and other community news.

Once again, we are a couple of betas – three in fact – further along than we were last time the blog came out. Let’s see what’s new in NVDA 2026.2 Beta 7 :

Changes introduced in Beta 7: Updates to translations Fix NVDA prompting to restart after updating, instead of logging off Revert SAPI5 bug fix from beta6 which was causing issues loading synthesizers Fix reading PDF content in Foxit PDF Editor with browse mode

Changes introduced in Beta 6: Updates to translations Show the restart dialog after updating from within NVDA, and make sure restarting offers the user the ability to save work in progress SAPI5 bug fix: skip over invalid voices rather than causing the entire driver to fail SAPI4 32-bit bug fix: support voices that don’t support pitch or rate Improve conflict handling between magnifier and screen curtain Restore the ability for add-ons to register custom touch modes in availableTouchModes

Changes introduced in Beta 5: Updates to translations Use math navigation category for one more math script Prevent NVDA freeze when brailling math with certain Unicode characters Improvements to Magnifier messages and settings names

Do head to the NVDA 2026.2 Beta 7 release announcement and try out the new beta. In fact, work is progressing well and we expect another beta to come out in the next few days.

We were recently asked about the “ Maximum Number of Characters on One Line ” setting. What does it do? And when might you change it?

Screenshot of NVDA’s browse mode settings

Ok, firstly, what is it? In a Word document or notepad text, the program exposes how much text is on one line. If you press down arrow, the caret moves to the character directly below. On the web, this isn’t as clearly defined. The size of the window, CSS rules, JavaScript, nearby images, and many other things can affect exactly how much text fits on a line. Because of this, and the way screen readers process web content, the document does not expose exactly where to move when you press down arrow. The way we work around this is to arbitrarily decide how many characters are on a “line”. There is a setting in NVDA’s browse mode settings called “Maximum number of characters on one line”. The default value for this is 100 characters. That is, when you press “down arrow”, the caret moves forward through the text on the web page by 100 characters.

As an example, the first line of the latest beta release announcement, visually, is: “Beta7 of NVDA 2026.2 is now available for download and testing. For” At NVDA’s default 100 max characters per line, pressing down arrow to that line will continue on to read “anyone who is interested in”, before stopping. If you change it to 50 chars, it will stop after “Available for” (it avoids stopping at half words).

The Beta 7 release announcement, used in the example above

NVDA user James also added: “When you’re not doing a say all and want to press Down Arrow less often, increase it. When you’re not doing a say all and would find it easier to process text in smaller chunks, decrease it.” Fellow NVDA user Pratik offered: “I have it set to maximum most times as well. If I want to read in smaller chunks, I do it with my Braille display. It’s a nice compromise.”

There is a companion setting, “Maximum lines per page” which, you can probably guess, adjusts how many lines the caret moves when you press page up or page down. The default for this is 25 lines.

How do you have these options set? Do continue the conversation on the Mastodon thread , or in the user group .

World Services for the Blind in the United States is one of many organisations around the world who provide training in NVDA. This is a valuable part of the job readiness program they provide. They recently invited us to collaborate with them on a webinar series introducing the new features of NVDA around the time of each release. We are very pleased to share with you, the inaugural “Access Point” webinar, with a focus on NVDA 2026.1 . We know many of our regular readers will be very familiar with what was new in NVDA 2026.1, as it has been out for nearly a couple of months now, but if you’d like a refresher, this could be the webinar for you. Starting something new always takes a little time to dial in, so we anticipate having the next version out a lot closer to when the stable NVDA 2026.2 is released.

We don’t often update features in ways which don’t change how they work. And, when we do, we don’t often highlight it. But let’s make an exception! NVDA has had a tool called the “COM registration fixing tool” for a long time now. We have covered it once before , and at the time noted that it could fix issues including: NVDA reports “unknown” when navigating in browsers such as Firefox, Thunderbird etc NVDA fails to switch between focus mode and browse mode NVDA is very slow when navigating in browsers while using browse mode

The tool can still fix all those and more, and it works much the same – but now it has a new name. Introducing: “System Accessibility Repair Tool”. The tool is a useful troubleshooting step any time you run into an unusual problem with NVDA. It is also one of the steps you are encouraged to make before reporting an issue on GitHub.

You can still find the System Accessibility Repair Tool on NVDA’s “Tools” menu. Press NVDA+n , then t for tools and you’ll find it listed there.

en.title: Beyond the Numbers: Do Flagship Processors Make a Real Difference in Daily Use?
en.summary: Android phones span a wide range of prices, starting at around $80 and reaching as high as $1,500. While it is not reasonable to expect…
en.body:
Published 13 July 2026 by Kareen Kiwan

Android phones span a wide range of prices, starting at around $80 and reaching as high as $1,500. While it is not reasonable to expect much from a low-end device, midrange phones have proven their place by offering good value for money, with reliable specifications that are more than sufficient for a lot of users without costing a fortune. Midrange devices now offer more RAM and storage than they did in previous years, and MediaTek, Samsung, and Qualcomm all offer capable processors that can comfortably handle light to moderate tasks.

In recent years, good midrange phones have typically been priced between $300 and $500. However, due to a combination of factors, prices are expected to increase across all price segments, making midrange devices more expensive and pushing the already hard-to-swallow prices of high-end devices even higher.

For nine years, I used midrange phones, including the Huawei P10 Lite, Huawei P30 Lite, Samsung Galaxy A71, and Samsung Galaxy A55, before switching to the Honor 600 Pro , which is powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite, the company’s flagship chipset from last year. It is still considered a very capable chipset today.

In this article, I will discuss the differences I noticed between using a high-end processor and a midrange one based on my personal experience. Rather than focusing on benchmarks, technical tests, or specifications, my goal is to talk about real-life daily usage and whether a flagship processor actually makes a meaningful difference.

Table of Contents

As blind users, we need a smooth and responsive screen reader experience on our devices. A screen reader needs to always be running on a blind user’s phone, requiring enough resources to remain responsive and reliable.

While noticeable lag should be expected on low-end devices, as these phones sometimes struggle with basic tasks even without a screen reader running, modern midrange devices are generally powerful enough to handle screen readers smoothly. For example, a sighted person I know owned an Honor X5b, a phone with very modest specifications, and used to wait several seconds when answering a call for the phone to react and display the call screen.

However, even with capable midrange processors, many Android users notice that screen readers are good overall but not perfect. There can be a short delay between touching the screen or swiping between onscreen elements and hearing the focused item announced. This delay becomes more noticeable when scrolling, as TalkBack needs time to identify the new items and place focus correctly.

Based on my own experience, moving to a high-end processor does not eliminate these delays, or at least the improvement is not dramatic. After switching from midrange phones to the Honor 600 Pro with Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite processor, I noticed some improvement in overall responsiveness. However, I am not even sure whether the difference I noticed is a real improvement or partly the placebo effect.

Since TalkBack is not my primary screen reader, I do not use it often. That said, my Accessible Android teammates who use TalkBack as their main screen reader report noticeably better performance on flagship devices, even if it is still not perfect.

Of the third-party screen readers available on Android, I only use Jieshuo , so I cannot comment on the experience with all other screen readers. From my experience, Jieshuo feels more responsive overall than TalkBack, especially while scrolling, although there is still room for improvement. Both TalkBack and Jieshuo offer the ability to reduce the delay between touching the screen and announcing the item under the finger, which improves this part of the experience. However, Jieshuo users should first determine whether this feature is reliable enough for them, as enabling it can still introduce issues in some situations.

Additionally, TalkBack improves typing responsiveness through the ability to reduce typing focus delay, while Jieshuo allows users to type with screen reader gestures suspended, which can positively affect typing speed.

In my opinion, the problem with screen reader performance on Android does not come from insufficient processor power, but rather from the communication between the operating system and the screen reader at the software level. There should be a review of how the necessary interactions between the system and accessibility services are handled in order to provide an almost lag-free experience across both midrange and high-end devices.

Unfortunately, many people, including myself, notice a difference in screen reader responsiveness when using VoiceOver on iOS devices, with interactions often feeling smoother and more immediate. This does not mean that the Android screen reader experience is poor. I have been an exclusive Android user for more than 13 years, and Android continues to meet my needs. However, improving screen reader responsiveness is always welcome, especially knowing that even midrange processors are already powerful enough to handle screen readers efficiently.

A lot of blind users rely on speech output from their screen readers to interact with their devices and access information. For those users, no matter how much screen reader responsiveness improves, a slow or unreliable TTS engine can ruin the entire experience.

With traditional TTS engines, I could not notice a meaningful difference between running them on a midrange device and on a high-end device. For example, Google Text-to-Speech performs similarly on both my Galaxy A55 and my Honor 600 Pro. Although it is the least responsive of the TTS engines I use, including Acapela, Vocalizer, and eSpeak, its responsiveness did not improve simply by moving to a more powerful processor.

However, with the emergence of neural and AI-based TTS engines, device performance starts to become more important. While none of the AI TTS engines currently available are ready to replace traditional engines as the primary daily screen reader TTS for most users, testing them, or using them to read articles or other content, is an interesting experience.

With these newer engines, I started to notice the limitations of a midrange processor. When testing ToBe SAID Pro on my Galaxy A55, powered by the Exynos 1480 processor, increasing the speech rate resulted in choppy speech, eventually reaching a point where the generated speech became almost impossible to understand. Even at lower speeds, speech interruptions could still occur sometimes.

Running the same engine on the Honor 600 Pro with the Snapdragon 8 Elite processor provided a noticeably better experience. I was able to increase the speech rate without experiencing the same issues, with the engine being able to generate speech quickly enough to keep up.

I also tested the Supertonic model through the BookFusion TTS engine. While the experience is still not completely smooth, the engine was usable. I have not tested this engine on my Galaxy A55, as the update supporting it was released recently, but I would expect the experience to be worse, with more lag and possible issues during speech generation.

Traditional TTS engines are still the most reliable choice regardless of the device being used. However, neural and AI-based engines are clearly here to stay, and they already demonstrate interesting capabilities. As these technologies continue to improve, processor performance may become increasingly important for blind users who want to take advantage of them.

Both midrange and high-end processors are capable of handling daily tasks, but the difference lies in the time it takes to complete certain operations, especially more complicated or intensive ones.

It is easy to notice the difference in the time required for the Play Store or third-party app installers to install the same application on a midrange and a high-end device. In-app tasks can also be completed faster with a more powerful processor. For example, converting a video to audio through the AudioLab app takes noticeably less time on a high-end device, with the difference being difficult to ignore.

It is worth keeping in mind, however, that some very demanding tasks can expose the limitations of a midrange processor, such as intensive gaming, advanced video editing, or other specialized workloads that many users may not need to perform regularly.

Opening apps and performing everyday tasks such as sending messages, making calls, and navigating through applications remain smooth and reliable on midrange devices, as they are already powerful enough to handle these tasks efficiently.

Even with many operations that are completed faster on high-end processors, waiting a few extra seconds for certain tasks on a midrange phone is still a trade-off worth considering, especially when taking into account the large difference in price between the two categories.

The processor, with both its CPU and GPU components, is a fundamental part of a device’s performance. It plays a major role in determining how well a phone handles daily tasks, ranging from basic operations to more advanced and resource-intensive ones. Its impact can also extend to other areas, such as the maximum connection speeds the device can achieve and the capabilities of other hardware features that depend on it.

However, the processor is not the whole story. A mobile phone is a complete package, and the final experience depends on the decisions made when designing the entire device. A powerful processor can deliver excellent performance, but other limitations can prevent it from showing its full potential.

For example, pairing a high-end processor with limited RAM or slower storage is like having a highly skilled manager without the right resources to work efficiently. The manager may be capable of handling complex tasks, but limited resources can prevent them from reaching their full potential. Poor thermal management can also reduce the advantage of a powerful processor, as the phone may need to throttle performance to control heat and continue operating safely. Battery capacity is another important factor. A high-end processor with a small battery is like having a powerful car with a tiny fuel tank.

Software is another important part of the equation. Poor optimization, crashes, stuttering, or badly optimized applications can make even the most powerful processor feel like a much lower-tier one. A great processor can only perform as well as the software around it allows.

Since the goal of this article is to provide an overview of the performance differences between a device running a high-end processor and one running a midrange processor, rather than to serve as a guide on what to look for when purchasing a new Android phone, I will not go into detail about every compromise manufacturers make to keep prices competitive, how those compromises affect users, or provide recommendations regarding purchasing decisions. It is worth noting, however, that midrange devices usually involve more compromises to achieve a lower price, while high-end phones tend to offer a more complete and well-rounded package.

With the current and expected price hikes, high-end phones are becoming harder and harder for many people to afford. At the same time, flagship killers are becoming closer to the flagships they were meant to challenge, with some now reaching the prices of last year’s high-end devices. Midrange devices are facing their own challenges, as manufacturers are expected to make more compromises to keep their devices within an affordable price segment.

While I cannot say that using a midrange device with a midrange processor is comparable to using a more powerful device with a flagship one, I can confidently say that the difference I experienced does not justify the large price gap for many people. Screen reader and TTS performance remain close between both categories, daily tasks can be performed reliably on both, and even when certain operations take longer on midrange processors, the extra waiting time is often a reasonable trade-off.

On-device AI is another area where high-end chipsets have an advantage, as running AI models locally requires powerful hardware. However, many AI features still rely on cloud processing, and the on-device features currently available are not yet valuable enough for many users to justify paying more.

Spending hundreds of dollars more is not always the best decision. In many cases, saving that money for something else can provide more value. You should not take a loan or put yourself under financial pressure just to buy a smartphone.

Before going beyond your budget, ask yourself: Do I really need the most powerful processor available? Would a larger battery make a bigger difference for my usage? What aspects of my phone experience do I value the most? What tasks do I perform regularly on my device?

Whether you are a blind or sighted user, you should not expect companies to make midrange devices identical to their high-end models. There needs to be a difference somewhere, with certain improvements reserved for more expensive devices. As a consumer, your purchase should be based on your needs and budget, while understanding that compromises and limitations are part of choosing a more affordable device. However, those limitations are often much smaller than the benefits gained from saving a considerable amount of money.

That being said, with manufacturers increasing the number of years of software support, looking at a high-end device released one or two years earlier can sometimes be a better choice than buying a new midrange device. This is because a previous-generation flagship processor will often remain more powerful than a current midrange processor.

At the end of the day, we all like to have the best and newest devices, but we must be wise and balance what we get with what we can afford and what we actually need.

Hola gente, ¿qué tal les va?

Muy atentos. Hoy les traigo la actualización de TCA-TTS-TIMMER, nuestro querido reloj parlante para Windows, que llega a la versión 1.2 cargada de novedades muy importantes y funcionalidades útiles!

Antes, para quienes no lo conozcan:

Es una pequeña utilidad desarrollada en Python que nos permite escuchar la hora cada 15 minutos, 30 minutos o cada hora, mediante un sonido y una voz TTS. Además, puede darnos la hora de muchos países de Latinoamérica y Europa, todo desde una interfaz sencilla, totalmente accesible y con atajos de teclado.

El reloj llega a la versión 1.2 con los siguientes cambios:

• Hora Universal UTC

Ahora el reloj incorpora un botón en la interfaz principal que te permite saber la Hora Universal UTC al instante. Disponible también mediante el atajo de teclado Alt+U. Muy útil para quienes trabajan con sistemas, servidores o simplemente necesitan la referencia horaria internacional.

• Nueva voz: Español México (mx)

Además de la voz español España, ahora incorporamos la voz español México (mx). Podrás elegir entre ambas desde el cuadro combinando "Lenguaje de la voz" en las opciones. Una voz clara y agradable que le da un toque diferente al reloj.

• Alarmas

¡TCA-TTS-TIMMER ahora permite establecer alarmas! Desde el botón "Alarmas" en la interfaz principal, podrás gestionar una o varias alarmas al día, eligiendo la hora, el sonido y el número de repeticiones. Ideal para recordatorios, descansos o lo que necesites.

• Apagado programado

Otra función muy solicitada: el apagado programado. Puedes programar que tu PC se apague automáticamente después de un número determinado de horas y minutos. Perfecto para cuando dejas el equipo realizando una tarea por la noche o antes de salir de casa. También incluye un botón para cancelar el apagado si cambias de opinión.

• Correcciones y mejoras internas

Se realizaron varias correcciones y mejoras en el código para un funcionamiento más estable y eficiente.

El programa es compatible con Windows 10 en adelante, para 64 bits. En versiones antiguas de Windows, puede que necesites las librerías Visual Studio C++ (incluidas en la descarga).

• El programa TCA-TTS-TIMMER 1.2 para 64 bits.
